entries.blurb: Search every file in a project in about the time it takes to blink. Most other search tools now measure themselves against it.
Find files without looking up find's syntax again. Sensible defaults and flags you can remember.
Read and reshape JSON right in the terminal, so you stop pasting API responses into a browser tab.
Read a file in the terminal with syntax colours and line numbers instead of a wall of grey text.
A directory listing that shows sizes, dates and git status in a layout you can scan at a glance.
Pick anything by typing a few letters of it: a file, a branch, or a command you ran last week.
The version control nearly every project assumes you have. Worth installing even though macOS bundles an older copy.
Open a pull request, review one, or check whether CI passed without leaving the terminal.
A visual way to stage, commit and rebase for the days when raw git commands stop being enjoyable.
Loads a project's environment variables the moment you step into its folder, and unloads them when you leave.
Send an HTTP request and actually read the answer, without assembling a line of curl flags first.
A code editor with an extension for essentially every language you are likely to pick up.
A terminal you can genuinely configure: split panes, saved profiles, and a search that works.
Snap windows into halves and quarters with a keyboard shortcut, the way you keep wishing macOS would.
Launch apps, run small scripts and search your clipboard history from a single keyboard shortcut.
Keep notes as plain Markdown files you own, with links between them that still work in ten years.
Convert, trim or re-encode almost any audio or video file. It is the engine inside most apps that claim to do this.
Resize, crop or convert a whole folder of images in one command instead of one file at a time.
Save a video or a podcast episode to watch later, on a train or anywhere else without a connection.
Open and create 7z archives, along with most other archive formats someone might send you.

categories.title: Keeping an eye on your Mac

entries.blurb: See what is using your processor, memory and network in a display you can read at a glance.
Find out what is actually filling your disk, sorted with the biggest offenders first.
Walk into the folder eating your disk space and delete things from the same screen.
Put processor, memory, network and battery readouts in the menu bar where you will notice them.
Remove an app together with the preference and cache files it quietly scattered around your disk.
